explanations.answer: Her righteousness shines like a bright light
explanations.explanation: That's the finish line verse 1 sets: “…until her righteousness shines like a bright light, her salvation like a blazing torch.” Until then, the speaker won't keep still. That's a LOT of standing around not sitting down. My mustache gives out after one batch of cookies.

explanations.answer: Her enemies run far from her gates
explanations.explanation: Enemies running off would make a nice ending, but it's not what verse 1 says. The speaker keeps going until her righteousness shines like a bright light. Enemies do come up later, in verse 8, where the LORD swears that her grain will never again go to them for food. That's a different promise from this one.

explanations.answer: Her broken walls are built back up
explanations.explanation: Walls do show up in this message, but not in verse 1. Here the speaker keeps going until her righteousness shines like a bright light. Walls come in verse 6, where watchmen are posted on them. Easy to mix up, since the whole message is about Jerusalem.

Verse 2 says it plainly: “…a new name that the mouth of the LORD will bestow.” The name comes straight from Him. I know a little about getting a name from somebody else. The Millers, the family who bought me for a quarter, carved Dorin on my handle, and I've worn it proudly ever since.
Nice try, but verse 2 doesn't hand the job to a prophet. It says, “…a new name that the mouth of the LORD will bestow.” The name comes from the LORD Himself. Nobody else is passing it out.

If the people picked the name, we'd need a group chat, forty-seven votes and one person who wants to rename everything. That's not what happens here. Verse 2 says, “…a new name that the mouth of the LORD will bestow.” The LORD gives it.

Verse 3 says it: “You will be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, a royal diadem in the palm of your God.” Notice where the crown is. It's held, not set down somewhere. Most of us can't even hold onto our car keys, and here's a crown being carefully held.

This one's true, friend. Verse 3 says, “You will be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, a royal diadem in the palm of your God.” So Zion is the crown, and it's in the LORD's hand. Easy to talk yourself out of it when it sounds this fancy.
This one's false, friend. Verse 4 says, “No longer will you be called Forsaken…” The old name is on its way out, and so is Desolate for her land. A brand new name is coming in its place.
Right, because verse 4 says, “No longer will you be called Forsaken…” Her land won't be named Desolate anymore either. Those two names get retired. Hephzibah and Beulah are stepping in.

explanations.answer: The LORD will take delight in her
explanations.explanation: Right after the new names, verse 4 gives the reason: “…for the LORD will take delight in you…” So the name comes with a reason attached. That's more than I can say for most names. Mine came with a price sticker.

explanations.answer: Her people will finally deserve it
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say a word about deserving. The reason it gives is this: “…for the LORD will take delight in you…” So it's all about the LORD's delight. Nothing in the text points to anyone earning it.

explanations.answer: Her old name will be forgotten
explanations.explanation: The old name does get dropped, since verse 4 says, “No longer will you be called Forsaken…” But that isn't the reason given for Hephzibah. The reason comes next: “…for the LORD will take delight in you…” Delight is the answer here.

Verse 5 says, “…as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.” Think of a groom at the front of the room who cannot stop grinning. That's the picture. Rejoicing is the word the text uses.

Watching shows up in this passage, but it's the watchmen on the walls, and that's verse 6. In verse 5 the word for the bridegroom is different. It says, “…as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.”

No weeping anywhere in this verse, friend. Verse 5 pictures a happy wedding: “…as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.” The word is rejoice, and that's the whole mood.
This one's false, friend. Verse 6 says of the watchmen, “…they will never be silent day or night.” That's the night shift with no quiet hour. I'd be asking about the coffee.
Right. Verse 6 says of the watchmen, “…they will never be silent day or night.” Day or night, no quiet time. That's a job with no break room.

explanations.answer: He makes Jerusalem the praise of the earth
explanations.explanation: Verse 7 gives the stopping point: “…until He establishes Jerusalem and makes her the praise of the earth.” Until then, they keep calling on Him. So it's a long, steady knock on the door. And the text tells us just where it ends.

explanations.answer: The watchmen come down off the walls
explanations.explanation: The text never says the watchmen come down. Verse 6 says of them, “…they will never be silent day or night.” The ending for those who call on the LORD is in verse 7: “…until He establishes Jerusalem and makes her the praise of the earth.”

explanations.answer: The harvest is brought in at last
explanations.explanation: Harvest does come up in this passage, but it's in verse 9 and it's a separate promise. The stopping point for those who call on the LORD is in verse 7: “…until He establishes Jerusalem and makes her the praise of the earth.”

Yes. In verse 8 the LORD says, “Never again will I give your grain to your enemies for food…” He swears it by His right hand and His mighty arm. That's a promise with a lot of weight behind it. The grain stays with the ones who worked for it.
This one's true, friend. In verse 8 the LORD says, “Never again will I give your grain to your enemies for food…” He swears it by His right hand and His mighty arm. The word to watch is never.

Verse 9 says it: “For those who harvest grain will eat it and praise the LORD, and those who gather grapes will drink the wine in My holy courts.” The ones who did the work get the meal. And they praise the LORD while they eat. I'd call that a good setup.

This one's true, friend. Verse 9 says, “For those who harvest grain will eat it and praise the LORD, and those who gather grapes will drink the wine in My holy courts.” The harvesters eat the grain. Praise goes right along with the meal.
Verse 10 says, “Go out, go out through the gates; prepare the way for the people!” So it's road work with a purpose. Think orange cones and a very long to-do list. The road is for the people.
Kings do get a mention in this passage, in verse 2, where they see Zion's glory. But the road in verse 10 isn't for them. It says, “Go out, go out through the gates; prepare the way for the people!”
No army in sight, friend. Verse 10 says, “Go out, go out through the gates; prepare the way for the people!” Nobody's marching here. The highway is for the people.

Verse 10 ends with the call to “…raise a banner for the nations!” A banner is made to be seen, so this is for everybody looking from outside. Nations came up in verse 2 too, where they see Zion's righteousness.
The watchmen are busy on the walls in verse 6, but the banner isn't for them. Verse 10 says, “…raise a banner for the nations!” Nations are the ones meant to see it.
Harvesters get their moment in verse 9, eating the grain and praising the LORD. But the banner is for somebody else. Verse 10 says, “…raise a banner for the nations!”

explanations.answer: To the ends of the earth
explanations.explanation: Verse 11 says, “Behold, the LORD has proclaimed to the ends of the earth…” That's as far as the earth goes. It's a message with a very long delivery route. And it's a message for Daughter Zion.

Gates are in this passage, in verse 10, where the call is to go out through them. But the proclamation in verse 11 goes much farther. It says, “Behold, the LORD has proclaimed to the ends of the earth…”

The holy courts are in verse 9, where the grapes are gathered and the wine is drunk. This proclamation reaches a lot further. Verse 11 says, “Behold, the LORD has proclaimed to the ends of the earth…”
Verse 11 says, “…See, your Savior comes!” That's the news carried to the ends of the earth. I think it's the kind of news that makes you drop everything and look. And the very next line has more.
A messenger would be a fine thing to expect, but that's not the word in verse 11. It says, “…See, your Savior comes!” The one coming is the Savior.
Harvest is in this passage, in verse 9, with grain and grapes. But the message for Daughter Zion in verse 11 is something else: “…See, your Savior comes!”
Verse 12 says, “…you will be called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken.” Sought out is the opposite of left behind. Somebody went looking. Forsaken had a good run, but the name changes.
Made Whole sounds like it could fit, but it's not in the text. Verse 12 says, “…you will be called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken.” Sought Out is the name given.
Set Free sounds like a great slogan, but it's not the name in this passage. Verse 12 says, “…you will be called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken.” That's the name that replaces Forsaken.
